speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
With the consent of the house I should like this notice of motion to stand until after eight o'clock.
Notice of motion stands.

In the absence of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. MacLaren), I have been asked to explain to the house the amendment made by the Senate. Hon. members will remember that this bill was very hurriedly reprinted and that in some cases reference to other boards had been omitted. Those omissions were corrected in the Senate. They are four in number, three of which refer to the original bill as presented to the committee over which I presided and the other is on account of an agreement between the Minister of Finance and the members of the British Empire Legion. The first amendment is on page 4 of the bill. While provision is here made that a quorum travelling in the country shall be comprised of two members of the board, there was no provision made for a quorum transacting ordinary routine business in Ottawa, and the result therefore would have been that under ordinary circumstances the quorum would have consisted of one-half erf the whole body which, if it consisted of twelve members, would compel six of them to remain continuously in Ottawa to hear routine business. The Senate therefore moved to insert the following as subsection 4 of the new section 7:
(4) Except as herein otherwise expressly provided, for the purpose of exercising and performing the powers, authorities and functions vested in the commission, as distinct from a quorum thereof, under this act, the commission shall consist of two or more commissioners; and whenever under this act a quorum of the commission is referred to it shall mean a quorum as constituted under the provisions of section fifty-five of this act.
I think hon. members will understand that. It is simply to provide that for the transaction of ordinary routine business in Ottawa it will not be necessary to have more members present than are at present required under the board of pension commissioners; that is to say, two or more may decide any ordinary routine matter. This does not interfere at all with section fifty-five which provides for a quorum in the field. That is distinctly and positively provided for.
Criminal Code

The next amendment is on page 6 of the bill, amending the clause providing for the payment of a pension to those members who have previously to this time served on the commission or the court. It is proposed to insert in 10B (1) after the word "bodies" in line twenty-two the words "or as a member of the board of pension commissioners for Canada or of the pension tribunal." That is to say, the act will provide for service on either of these bodies being counted in the total service.
The next amendment is on page 13, and is a very simple one. It is with regard to the presentation of cases to the chief pensions advocate. The amendment is to insert after the word "before" in line ten on page 13 the words "the commission or." I think my hon. friend from Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) will understand that. It simply means that the applicant has the power to appear before either the commission itself or a quorum thereof.
The next amendment is on page 18, amending clause 63 by adding after the words "reference" in line five the words "or submission." Our committee found that it was necessary to allow the applicant to submit a stated case to the court, not necessarily the file, and consequently the words "or submission" have been inserted.
The next amendment is on page 21, and this is the one which applies to the agreement entered into 'between the Minister of Finance and the representatives of the soldier organizations. It was never intended that the prospective pension of a dependent mother or father, or brother or sister, under section 33 of the act should be limited, and consequently the Senate have struck out in line eighteen on page 21 the words "or section thirty-three." Those words were evidently placed in there under a misapprehension, and I am sure the house will agree that this amendment is perfectly proper.

not apply to widows.

It is prospective pensions to dependent parents and brothers and sisters. They are now being left out of the clause which restriots their pension, and the amendment now is so that they will not be affected by this act or by the budget proposals which were originally made by the Minister of Finance.

speakeroldname: Hon. MAURICE DUPRE (Acting Minister of Justice) moved:
speechtext:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours that this house disagrees with their amendment to Bill No. 71, an act to amend the criminal code for the following reason:
Because the wording of the said amendment may be deemed to involve a principle which it may not be advisable to sanction in an act of parliament, and that the clerk do carry the said message to the Senate.
Explain.

After this house had accepted section 3 of Bill No. 71, to amend the criminal code, the Senate deleted subsection

Canada Shipping Act
3 of section 3 which concerns an irrebuttable presumption. That was sent back to the Senate and the whole bill came back again to this house with subsection 3 reinserted and subsection 2 amended. Subsection 2 in the bill as it left this house reads:
Every person who, in the home of a_ child, participates in adultery, or in sexual immorality, or indulges in habitual drunkenness or any other form of vice, thereby endangering the morals of such child or rendering the home of such child an unfit place for such child to be in shall be guilty of an offence and liable, upon summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars, or to imprisonment for a period not exceeding one year, or to both fine and imprisonment.
In order to cover the second case, namely that of a man and a woman living in adultery, where the children might be affected, the Senate added a proviso to subsection 2 which reads as follows:
Provided that this subsection shall not apply in the case of two persons who though in fact living in adultery are living apparently respectably as man and wife, and where the children affected are the children of such union.
That is free love.

As this amendment or proviso might be considered as a sort of indirect consecration of adultery, we believe it would be advisable to have another drafting or another sort of amendment to subsection 2.
Motion agreed to.

So far as I could hear from this point in the chamber we might have been dealing with the redistribution bill. I have no intention of delaying the house when we should be home. This subsection deals with five sections in the original bill. They cover safety regulations. It was because these details were in the bill that I voted for it, although I was well aware that the primary object of the bill as the minister said was to institute a monopoly on the great lakes, objection to which has been voiced by hon. members to my left and right.
No.
He did not say that.

The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis) truly pointed out that while the provisions of this bill in relation to the great lakes come into effect the moment it is passed, the operation of the provisions relating to the safety regulations is postponed indefinitely. I also note with some apprehension that while there is provision for appointing inspectors there is no provision for paying them. That makes one wonder how remote the appointment of these men will be. On the second reading of the bill I did not, of course, criticize these regulations, but I criticized, and I think justly, the method in which this bill was introduced so late in the session, not being sent to a committee where it could be adequately discussed, and no chance allowed to get the views of the men concerned. The men in British Columbia do not even know that this bill has been introduced. For this the Minister of Trade and Commerce took me somewhat severely to task, in language that I think went somewhat beyond the range of parliamentary usage or the dignity that one expects from a cabinet minister-or that we used to expect from a cabinet minister. The minister, when he sat on this side of the house, built up a reputation for fair and logical debate. I must say that I think he rather lessens that reputation when he takes a position of political infallibility, that if anything he sets his signature upon is criticized from the opposite side, the wretched member must be doubly and trebly damned.
Oh, I never said that.

I do not think that is a
desirable attitude. I suggest to the minister that he follow the attitude of his own leader

Canada Shipping Act
who the other day said quite frankly when the opposition was putting forward some criticism,-I noted it particularly,-that the criticism put forward by the opposition had a good deal of point to it and was such as he himself would have made had he sat on the opposite side. The Minister of Finance, and also I think the Minister of Public Works, have not once, but several times stated in this house that they were quite ready to welcome criticism. The tolerant point of view, that it is just possible someone else may be sincere in holding a different view, makes for the amenities of public life and certainly facilitates the passage of legislation. Personally I absolutely decline to submit to such dictation; this house is still democratic, whatever the government may be, and I propose to maintain as well as I can the rights of the private members of parliament.
Turning to the minister in charge of this bill, the hon. Minister of Marine, I am glad to second the remark of the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) last night that he always treats criticism with fairness and courtesy. These safety regulations are going to be put into effect, as we find by subsection 681A, by regulations made by the governor in council. I am sorry to see that. It is all to be done by regulation. Why is it not definitely included in the act? This is another instance of what we have seen done so often, our jurisdiction taken away and handed over to the minister, which often means not the minister but his deputy or officials, a bureaucracy which we cannot control. There are two functions of government, the legislative and the executive. We are continually handing over a little more and a little more of our legislative powers either to the cabinet or to some member or official thereof. We have had three glaring instances of that evil this present session. I will not take time to mention any but the last, that is in connection with radio. We gave the government or the radio commission power to make regulations, and I am perfectly certain, and I think every hon. gentleman must be of the same opinion, that if we had been passing those regulations in this house a lot of them would never have been passed in the language which we criticized and commented on a couple of days ago. Now we are doing the same thing here, putting power into the hands of a department to legislate. Not to carry out our decision, but we give them the power, by order in council and regulation, to legislate differently to what perhaps we would do! Why not put it in the act? Perhaps have a general clause giving a little leeway, but the main features should be in the act.
Then I notice that the regulations are to have regard to the following things, and there are one, two, three, four, five-really only four, because the last does not apply to safety-four matters on which they are going to make regulations. They are somewhat vague. As far as they go they are all right, but they do not go far enough. I want to put on record one or two other details that should engage the attention of the department in drawing up these regulations, in the hope that when they come to draw them up they will include them also, although I am a little doubtful as to their power to do so. I am quoting from a memorandum prepared by the Vancouver harbour commissioners some time in 1931. I am only going to quote a few paragraphs:
No block nor shackle shall be rigged directly over the head of a workman if it can possibly be avoided.
No man shall be required to work m holds with the hatches off whilst other work or loading or unloading is proceeding above them unless conditions are such as to preclude anything falling from an upper deck injuring those who are working below.
That is not referred to in the act, and I know a man who was killed a year ago by lack of that precaution.
All vessels loading or unloading shall have each hatch that is working tended by a competent hatch tender.
That is not in the bill.
When the vessel is either loading or unloading lumber-
And this is where I am interested.
-or any long loose material such as round pipes, steel rods, rails, etc., and only one sling is being used on each load, the sling shall be of sufficient length to permit a round turn on the load.
That is a very necessary thing.
In vessels loading a deckload of lumber, logs, piling or poles, the deck load shall be secured by hog lashings at a height of not more than six feet from the level of the deck and every four feet thereafter.
The next one has a similar bearing.
No man shall be permitted to work below walled timber, lumber-
That is piled up timber.
-logs, poles or piling unless such wall has been so secured as to preclude the wall or any part of it falling into the space in which the man is working.	_
Any vessel loading or unloading from or to booms, rafts or cribs shall supply a rowboat equipped with a lifebuoy and pike pole and have it attended by a competent person.
Canada Shipping Act

In many cases that is done voluntarily but it ought to be compulsory.
Men shall not be permitted to go into the holds of vessels after such holds have been fumigated until the holds have been certified in writing, by the officer responsible, to be clear of gas.
Those are all things that, as far as I can see, could not be covered by even the broad provisions of the bill. But they certainly should be there.
Another fault I have to find is that there has been omitted a clause often found in such bills which would go a long way to compensate for the absence of the things I have suggested. I have not got the legal language, but the lawyer members will understand what I mean. I am speaking of a clause something like this: Without restricting the generality of the above section attention is directed to the following items. That is not the technical wording, but all lawyers know that if you do not have a clause like that, the working of the act is confined entirely to the items that are mentioned, whereas if a general clause is put in it is not so restricted and it would be possible to go further with the regulations than the details mentioned in the act. That clause certainly ought to be in, and I submit to the minister that he might as well have it put in now. It is not a question of expense, it is a question of making the act more workable.
I have just one more objection. In subsection 2 of 681a penalties not exceeding $100 and not less than $50 are provided for anyone contravening any regulation made under this section. That penalty is simply ridiculous.
I took the trouble to look it up and I find that we have this year on two occasions-I have it under my hand if anyone wants to see it-imposed for a much less serious thing than where men's lives are at stake a possible penalty of $2,000 and not less than $200 and a possible gaol term as well of not less than three months. If the $2,000 is not paid the offender is liable to a further gaol term of not less than three months. What was the crime involved there? In the one case it was being in possession of liquor that had been made illegally, that is, without having a licence. If a man or some poor ignorant woman made a little home brew and did not know that a licence was required, he or she would be liable to a fine of $2,000 and to a gaol term of not less than three months. Here the lives of men are at stake, but if a life is lost through neglect to provide these safeguards, on the first offence the fine is only $50.

Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, many of these accidents are fatal. If a stick of timber is dropped down two holds and falls on a man he has not much chance to survive, or if a man falls backward into a hold through the lack of a proper guard, his life may be lost. Let me give another instance. Many of these ships are loaded and unloaded in a hurry; perhaps they must pay demurrage if they are not at another port in so many days. There is a rush, and sometimes these safety provisions do take a little while to rig up, and possibly they may cause a little delay in the handling of the cargo. Under such conditions it would pay the ship owner to take a chance and drive his men on in order to get through, ignoring the provisions of the act. If the ship is loaded without accident the owner is that much ahead; he has got away with it and saved expense. But if something should go wrong and a man should lose his life, for the first offence the ship owner would get off with a fine of only $50. Most ships load a couple of hatches at the same time, and in such a case the wage bill would be more than $100 an hour. It would pay a ship owner to take a chance in order to save half an hour's wages. I think we are making a burlesque of the matter when we impose the extreme fine of $100 for an offence which may cost a man his life. Surely there should be some greater severity and some heavier penalty than a fine of $50 in the first instance.
I think that is a most regrettable feature.
I intend to propose an amendment when we reach section 681d. Perhaps I should wait until we reach that section; if you say I should do so, Mr. Chairman, I will wait. Section 681d reads:
The expression "tackle," as used in the four sections immediately preceding means the tackle, machinery, gear, apparatus and appliances used on board a ship for the loading or unloading thereof.
That is not the way the section was introduced originally; the Senate changed the wording, and I should prefer to go back to the section as it was drafted by the officials of the department. I think the latter part should read:
-gear, apparatus and appliances used for the loading or unloading of ships, and includes all tackle whether on ship or on shore.
The difference, of course, is that in the one case it is confined to the tackle on the ship, and in the other case it applies to tackle on shore or on the wharf as well. This is very necessary, because vessels are often

Canada Shipping Act
loaded by an engine with a derrick, placed on the wharf or on the bank of a river. If the object is to protect the lives of the men this provision is equally necessary whether the defective crane, we will say, is on the boat itself or whether it is on the wharf or the bank of the river. It is suggested that this is beyond our jurisdiction and that, being on land, this tackle would come under provincial authority. The minister was kind enough to discuss this question with me last night, and he said there were provincial officials who were charged with such inspection. All I can say with regard to British Columbia-and I consulted with my colleague from South Vancouver-is that we never heard of any official who performed duties of that kind. There are officials appointed under the workmen's compensation board who go into the woods and supervise the machinery used there, but I do not think their jurisdiction extends to cases such as these. Further than that, the objection is surely overcome by the fact that under the old act the inspection extended to the shore. Section 674 reads:
-may inspect and examine the tackle, machinery or apparatus used for the loading or unloading thereof.
It seems to me we are going back if we limit it to the tackle on board ship when the old act, which we are trying to improve, said the inspection extended to all tackle used for loading or unloading, which would cover tackle on shore.
While I am on my feet there is just one other point I should like to impress upon the minister, also in regard to these regulations. I should like the hon. gentleman to give us some assurance-and I do not see why he should not do so-that when these regulations are formulated, and I hope he will indicate .that this will foe done in the near future, they will be published in the Canada Gazette so that everyone .may know exactly what the regulations are. If the minister would be kind enough to assure me on those two points I will wait until we come to section 691d to imove the amendment I have suggested. 1

Before the minister replies .may I say that I agree almost entirely with everything that has been said by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi in connection with Ithese amendments. Of course that does not include his reference to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in his opening remarks. The need for these amendments has been so apparent to those engaged in this work that I think we should take every care to see that
they are made as precise as possible. Section 681 seems a little indefinite. It says:
The governor in council may from time to time appoint at such places in Canada as he deems advisable-
I believe this could be strengthened by .making it read:
The governor in council may and shall from time to time appoint at such places in Canada as he deems advisable-
The same change might be made in section 681a, which reads:
The governor in council may make regulations for the protection against accident of workers employed in loading or unloading ships-
I suggest that this should read:
The governor in council may and shall make regulations for the protection^ against accident of workers employed in loading or unloading ships-
I believe this change should be made because, as I said yesterday, there has been a great deal of objection on the part of stevedoring companies and shipping federations against the taking of any but the very least precautions for safety in loading and unloading ships. I have before me a letter from the shipping federation of British Columbia to the Deputy Minister of Marine, dated August 23, 1932, in which they regretted that the minister was taking steps to engage an inspector of tackle who would see that safety regulations were carried out. I am sure these objections will continue, and I think for the protection of the minister himself the act cannot be made too strong or too definite. Let me repeat that I agree entirely with the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni with regard to these amendments.

I should like to make just a few observations with regard to this portion of the bill. While I take no great exception to the observations of the bon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), I should like to direct the attention of the committee to the words which he complains are out of order or impose a strain on the decorum of the house, so that I might at least be in the judgment of the committee whether or not I conduct my discussions with due regard to the amenities of parliament. The words to which the hon. member referred were these -I am quoting from Hansard, page 5119, reporting the debate on the same bill:
The hon. member for _ Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) in his usual sarcastic manner-
Mr. Neill: Thank you.
Canada Shipping Act

Mr. Stevens: -referred to this part of the bill in most scathing terms. I think his remarks were entirely unjustifiable. There is nothing mysterious about the nautical or shipping terms used in the bill-
Read further.

Yes, further down there
is this:
The hon. gentleman is not the only man in the house or in the world who has a fairly wide knowledge of many of these things, and I would suggest to him that he would have been serving those whose interests he frequently pretends to have at heart-
Hear, hear.

Then I was interrupted
and I went on:
I say, he would have been serving much better those whose interests he has at heart had he said a word of commendation to the minister for at least the attempt to bring in these measures providing for safety appliances in the ports.
If there is anything offensive in parliamentary debate in the words I have quoted-
"Pretends"?

-I fancy that hon. members who take exception to discussion of that sort will have great difficulty in carrying on debate at all. I simply say this. As the hon. member who has taken his seat knows, this measure is of great interest to the men working in the hazardous calling of loading and unloading ships in various parts of Canada, and particularly I think in the great port of Vancouver. He has raised the matter here and so have I over a period of years, and as I said the other day, it was hoped that we might have done something in this regard last year. But for reasons which it is useless now to discuss the bill was not then proceeded with. Then we included the present proposals in the general revision of the aot this year; but when it was found, for purely constitutional reasons, that we could not proceed with the main act, the minister excerpted from that act these separate provisions relating to pilotage and to lake shipping, and it was considered that, these three matters being of sufficient urgency, we should bring in a separate bill this year instead of putting the whole matter off until next year.
Under these circumstances I submit that the minister ought to have been commended rather than criticized for his action. Now with regard to the observations that have just been made with reference to those measures in the bill dealing with inspection, the minister himself will discuss them from a technical point of view, but I am speaking now as one 
who for twenty years represented one of the largest ports in Canada and who therefore is deeply interested in the success of this legislation. The observations of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni indicated more clearly than I could in half an hour's argument the imperative necessity of empowering the governor in council to direct these matters by making regulations, because the hon. gentleman cited a number of more or less minor details which illustrate that there must be thousands of such. If we were to put them all in the bill, if we embodied them in the bill in detail, we should probably find ourselves limited to the terms of the bill, with the result that such contingencies as were not actually indicated in the bill would not come within the purview of the inspectors. Under the bill however, and following universal practice in this respect -the practice in other countries and the practice dictated by many of the major statutes of Canada-we have empowered the governor in council to make regulations. Let me read the section as it is here:
681a. The governor in council may make regulations for the protection against accident of_ workers employed in loading or unloading ships,-
Let us stop right there. That is very broad, and it is a general injunction imposed upon the minister and the governor in council to make regulations of a general character for the protection of those employed in the loading and unloading of ships, and I submit to the committee that this includes everything in the way of risks which might crop up unexpectedly-risks unforeseen in the loading or unloading of ships. It goes on:
-having regard in particular to the following:-
And "the following" are matters that are again fairly broad.
(a)	the strength of machinery, tackle and gear and their fitness for the purpose for which they are intended;
That embraces all apparatus used-ropes, cables, blocks and tackle, winches, booms and so forth, everything used in the loading or unloading of ships. All these are subject to the regulations to be made by the governor in council.
(b)	the provision of proper safe gangways, stagings and matters of a like character.
This provision anticipates a peculiar class of accident which I regret to say is frequent on the Pacific coast. Late at night in the dark men have on many occasions fallen off the edge of the dock or off an unprotected deck space on the ship, falling between the ship and the dock; and usually, lying be-

tween the ship and the dock, are a couple of large booms, probably three or four feet thick, thirty feet below the level of the dock or of the deck of the ship. Men have not uncommonly fallen down between the ship and the dock and been killed or seriously injured; frequently they are drowned. This provision is intended to take care of such accidents.
The next subsection provides:
(e) protection in the way of rails or other sufficient protection at openings through decks and around wharves and docks.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni suggested that this did not refer to the protection of hatchways. I submit that it covers that very matter. Where there is a hatchway open it usually has a combing and roping around which may be and usually is set up, and this provides that it shall be done. It is provided here that suitable protection shall be given to safeguard against risks of that kind. The next subsection reads:
(d) illumination of holds and decks of ships, and docks or wharves at which ships may be loading or unloading.

On subsection 932-British ships.

Before dealing with this section I should like to say that I differ with many hon. members on this side of the house; I am absolutely in support of this bill, particularly with regard to the section relating to safety appliances. In regard to the section, now before the committee however, I should like to direct a question to the minister. I know that under the British commonwealth merchant shipping agreement the registry of British ships is defined, and I should like to ask him why we have not followed the example set by Australia and New Zealand in this connection and defined the registry of British ships in Canada as it is defined in that agreement, which I might say was signed by Great Britain, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, the Irish Free State and Newfoundland. Under that agreement it is almost imperative that the persons owning or registering such ships shall be British subjects.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I suppose my hon.
friend has read section 1 of the Merchant Shipping Act of 1894, which says:
A ship shall not be deemed to be a British ship unless owned wholly by persons of the following description (in this act referred to as persons qualified to be owners of British ships); namely,-
(a)	Natural born British subjects;
(b)	Persons naturalized by or in pursuance of an act of parliament of the United Kingdom, or by or in pursuance of an act or ordinance of the proper legislative authority in a British possession;
(c)	Persons made denizens by letters of denization; and
(d)	Bodies corporate established under and subject to the laws of some part of Her Majesty's dominions, and having their principal place of business in those dominions:
Provided that any person who either-
(i)	being a natural born British subject has taken the oath of allegiance to a foreign sovereign or state or has otherwise become a citizen or subject of a foreign state; or
(ii)	has been naturalized or made a denizen as aforesaid;
shall not be qualified to be owner of a British ship unless, after taking the said oath, or becoming a citizen or subject of a foreign state, or on or after being naturalized or made denizen as aforesaid, he has taken the oath of allegiance to Her Majesty the Queen, and is during the time he is owner of the ship either resident in Her Majesty's dominions, or partner in a firm actually carrying on business in Her Majesty's dominions.
As we see, Great Britain has deliberately abstained from defining British ships by statute, and in the past Canada has done so by section 932 of the Canada Shipping Act. The present draft eliminates the word "means" from the definition and adds at the end the words "and are by the law of England" and so forth. So we follow the same practice that is followed in England at the present time. By the marine laws of England it is the place of control in fact of a ship owned by a corporation, and not the place of residence or the nationality of the owners of the shares of the corporation, or even the place of registration of such a ship, that settles the nationality of the vessel.

There is another point to
which I should like to direct the attention of the minister, and perhaps it might be discussed at this time because it is of great importance to many seamen on the Pacific coast. Subject to any special provisions that may be made by any part of the commonwealth as to the qualifications to be required of officers on ships engaged in its coasting trade,-
The next words are those to which I wish to refer.
-a valid certificate of competency or service granted by one part of the commonwealth will be recognized throughout the British commonwealth as indicating that the holder is duly qualified accordingly when serving on board any ship registered in that part.

It happens that I received the same affidavits to which the hon. gentleman has referred. They were prepared by the Seamen's Union. The complaint is of course a very natural one. committee that they are now being carefully looked into. We feel that these men are entitled to have the whole matter fully surveyed, and at the moment we can make no statement. May I hazard one or two observations, not for the purpose of justifying the attitude of the ship's captain but rather that we may have before us at least part of the argument to be advanced on the other side. A British ship comes to the harbour of Vancouver with a British crew, or at any rate a crew taken on at a British port, and as the result of desertion, or possibly discharge or sickness, they may be short a few men. Usually the crew is signed on for the round trip, wherever they may be going-sometimes around the world, sometimes from Liverpool to Vancouver and return, whatever the cruise may be. Frequently on arriving at Vancouver the ship will be short three or four men. The master of a British ship in such a situation will go to the shipping master and ask for a sufficient number of men to complete his crew. The affidavit asserts that these captains have been instructed not to employ Canadian sailors. I submit that that statement in that form looks prejudicial to Canadian interests, but I apprehend that this is the more correct way to put it. Inasmuch as there are a very large number of British born seamen who are themselves unemployed in these days, the owners of the vessels in Great Britain desire that their captains in signing on men in any port away from home-a port in one of the dominions, for instance-should give the preference to British sailors entitled to return to Great Britain, thus finishing a cruise which had been broken in some way. I presume therefore, speaking again without absolute knowledge, that the instructions are not to bring back any man who will not be completing a voyage and who, on his arrival in Liverpool, may be subject to discharge, simply adding to the ranks of the unemployed there. They prefer therefore to bring back if possible British seamen who are competent, shall I say, to finish the voyage in Liverpool in the ordinary course of events.
I am quite certain that neither the British government nor the British board of trade, under which these regulations very largely come, has ever at any time given instructions that Canadian or Australian seamen, or seamen from any of [DOT] the other dominions shall be treated prejudicially or in any unfair way.

This movement of grain to Buffalo is of two general distinct characters. One is during the open season of navigation when grain moves freely from the head of the lakes to the seaboard by Canadian and United States ports. It will move to Buffalo and naturally be moved as rapidly as possible through to New York, Boston, Providence, Portland, Baltimore, Philadelphia and other ports where it can find the cheapest and best shipping to carry it to the markets of the world. The consequence is that during that period the tendency is to push the grain through. But when we come down toward the end of navigation, the holders of wheat will very frequently, in fact every year, store up as much as they can in Buffalo and hold it there because, as I said the other day, it is a good kicking-off place. The tendency is to do that, but that is for what we call winter storage. In addition to putting the grain into elevators, it is a common practice to rent storage in as -many vessels as they can and tie those vessels up to docks contiguous to an elevator spout to be loaded in the winter or spring as the case may be. Those vessels are frozen in and remain there as winter storage. Precisely the same thing applies to Port Col-borne, Port McNicoll, Midland, Goderich and other bay ports.
What we were discussing the other day was this principle: Is it possible or competent for a shipper of Canadian grain through Buffalo to Great Britain to earn the preference? I have stated over and over again: Yes, it is, provided he observes the terms of regulation No. 12 of the British Imports Act. Regulation No. 12 in brief is this, that not merely wheat, but goods of any kind, of course including wheat, shipped from a British territory or a fMr. Stevens.]
British dominion through a foreign country must, in order to earn the preference in Great Britain, be consigned through on a through bill of lading. Then it says further, that in the absence of a through bill of lading, it must have such invoices and other documents as may be certified by the customs authority in the foreign country to show that the goods were shipped through in a direct route from the point of shipment in a British territory to Great Britain. Any wheat or any other commodity that is handled in that fashion will earn the preference.
Let us pause for a moment and study, shall I say, the soundness or sanity of that. Obviously, neither Great Britain nor Canada nor any other country desires to place upon its statute books a preference and then make that preference open for goods that may lie in a foreign country for weeks, months or even years. There must be some control over the goods and so this provision that I have mentioned has been made.
When the wheat shipments were made last winter, this is what happened: Wheat had been moved from Port Arthur to Buffalo and put into storage. they are.

Oh no, the American shipping laws will not permit Canadian ships to take part in any American coastal trade. Let me give an instance. Last year or the year before there was a good deal of sulphur shipped from Texas up the Atlantic coast to Montreal and then transshipped and taken to some inland American port. The Canadian boats wished to share in that traffic but no Canadian boats could get in on it at all; the American shipping laws do not permit them to take part on one leg or the other in intercoastal shipping in the United States. That is the reason Canadian shipping wants to be put on the same basis. This bill merely does that and nothing more-not another thing beyond what the Americans have been doing to the Canadians for years. This is the first time that Canadian shipping is being put on the same basis as American, and it is only fair that dt should be. In regard to the remark of my hon. friend from Weyburn-
Before the hon. minister leaves that sulphur shipment, is it proposed now to refuse to let an American bottom come to the port of Montreal and do what they did with the sulphur?

No, certainly not. We do not interfere with that in the least. I was just giving that as an illustration of the intercoastal trade of the United States, in which they will not permit a Canadian ship to take part on either leg of the journey. We are only putting the wheat 'trade on the same basis. Previous to this bill an American ship could carry wheat to Buffalo and another American ship could take it thence to Montreal, so that they did both legs of the journey, but Canadians were not allowed to carry on either leg of a corresponding journey between American ports. Now we are putting them on the same basis.
I might give another illustration that came to my notice as Minister of Railways in regard to a large number of cargoes of coal shipped up the lakes. It is said that the Canadian ships are in a combine. The prices quoted for the carriage of that coal ran from 17 cents to 25 cents per ton. Seventeen cents is a ridiculously low rate, a losing rate, and some ships would not look at it, but the tenders ran from 17 to 25 cents; I think some were 20 and 22. That does not look much like a combine. The coal traffic is usually divided amongst them at the lowest rate. If there was anything in the shape of a combine
Canada Shipping Act

all they had to do was to get together and instead of tendering from 17 to 25 cents, all put in the 25 cent rate. That came to my notice within the last two weeks. It shows that there certainly is not a combine on the up journey. And by all the methods that the Minister of Marine has mentioned in this discussion the government can certainly prevent a combine on the down journey.

Has the minister seen the
by-laws of the Associated Lake Freighters?

I have not seen them
recently, but I am arguing the point without the by-laws; we have power through the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Marine and the board of grain commissioners and the shipping laws to break any such combine. And finally, if the Canadian shipowners take unfair advantage, this parliament can repeal the law. I do not think there would be a man on this side of the house who would not at once support the repeal if he thought the Canadian shipowners with their fifty-two ships were taking unfair advantage of this law in any shape or form. Surely every member of this committee is anxious for Canadian advantage; surely it is not the desire of the committee to give to American bottoms the right to drive Canadian bottoms out of the great lakes trade and put into the hands of American bottoms complete control of the carriage of Canadian grain, giving them power to charge any price they choose later on. Surely we do not wish entirely to destroy our Canadian shipping, but that is what is happening to-day. Anyone who has watched the price of the stock of the Canada Steamship Lines, which is the biggest line on the lakes, knows what is happening. This line has the largest fresh water ship in the world, the Lemorne, with a capacity of something like 600,000 bushels of grain. A few years ago the preference stock of the Canada Steamship Lines was selling at 84. Yesterday, out of curiosity, I checked it up, and I found that it was selling at 7. The reason is that the company is on the verge of going out of business; it cannot carry on with the present business that is being done. It is not getting the business, and I think it is only fair that we should want some Canadian shipping left.
The minister had better say they need volume.

That is what I said; they are not getting the business. If the United States vessels are allowed to come in and take it away from them they cannot carry on. After all-though my hon. friend will not (Mr. Manion.]
agree with this-the basis of protection is to give volume, not necessarily higher prices. If our Canadian ships, after they get the traffic, do not treat the farmers of the west fairly I for one, and I am sure I should be joined by all hon. members on this side of the house, would want to undo a law that harmed the farmers. I am not a farmer myself, but the head of the lakes is just as much interested in the success of the farmers as are the farmers themselves.
Will United States vessels still be permitted to carry grain consigned through United States ports?
Certainly.

Some time ago the minister gave the total capacity of the lake carriers as 14,000,000 bushels. Perhaps the minister, coming from the head of the lakes, will be able to answer this question: On the average how long does it take to make the trip from the head of the lakes and back?
To Montreal?
Average them all up.

It depends to a large extent on where the vessel is going. It is very much shorter to the Georgian bay ports than it is to Port Colborne; it is a great deal shorter to Port Colborne than to Prescott, and it is still farther to Montreal. Since the Welland canal has been deepened it is possible for the large boats to go as far as Prescott. I do not know what the average would be, and I would hardly care to make a guess.
Six days?

Yes, that would be my
guess if I cared to make one.
For the sake of argument we will say it takes six days, and we will assume that the lakes are open for twelve weeks in the fall.

I see what my hon. friend is coming to, and I do not wish to make a statement that I cannot support. I do not know that six days would be the average. It would be roughly a three day journey from the head of the lakes to Port Colborne, and of course it would take three days to go back. But they have to unload and they might be tied up waiting for other ships or for other reasons. They could not make it to Montreal and back in six days, so I should say that average is rather low.

All I want to point out is that if we had twelve weeks in the fall, in

Canada Shipping Act
the rush season, with that capacity we could only move 168,000,000 bushels. Would there not be some danger of congestion at the head of the lakes in that event?

Well, 168,000,000 bushels
is a lot of grain to move in three months.

Then let me ask the
minister this question: On the average how much is offered by the farmers of the west to the trade, and what is the total storage capacity at the head of the lakes?

There my hon. friend
comes up against the question of futures, as he knows. The only way the grain of the western farmers is taken care of, as far as offerings are concerned, is by the existence of the futures' market, and the grain is held by those who desire to go into that business. My hon. friend knows that last winter we held at the head of the lakes something like 68,000,000 bushels. I could look up the figures, if I had time, to show precisely the amount of grain that has been moved during the fall rush, but I do not think it applies to this argument.
May I reply to an observation made by the hon. member for West Edmonton, which I think should not go unchallenged. The hon. gentleman said the rate to Buffalo was two cents, and he went on to say that surely another two cents ought to cover the transportation to Montreal. I know the committee desires to be just and fair. The movement from the head of the lakes to Buffalo or any bay port is made in these large vessels. I will give the capacity of just a few; 420,000 bushels, 460,000 bushels, 350,000 bushels, 550,000 bushels, 220,000 bushels, 320,000 bushels and so on. The capacity of the ships below Niagara, however, is much less; some of them carry 95,000 bushels, 85,000 bushels, 82,000 bushels, 75,000 bushels, 100,000 bushels and so on, most of them less than 85,000 bushels. So the movement of grain over a short distance in a ship carrying 400,000 bushels is a much less expensive proposition than the handling of grain in a ship carrying only 70,000 or 80,000 bushels.
That is the first point. Then we must remember that with the exception of the Soo it is clear sailing from the head of the lakes to Buffalo or Port Colborne or the bay ports, but from Niagara down to Montreal the ships must pass through a long series of canals and looks. The difficulties in navigating these narrower and more difficult waters certainly are much more serious than is the case on the lakes. As a consequence the rates from Buffalo or Port Colbome to Montreal could not be expected to be anything like as low
as the rates from the head of the lakes to Buffalo. I think it is only fair to the shipping interests to point out these facts. I am definitely of the opinion that there is no ground for complaint when the rate from the head of the lakes is around six or seven cents a bushel, The present rate of four cents a bushel, while no doubt a good rate for those shipping the grain, certainly is most unprofitable for the carriers.

I want to take the minister back to where this discussion started. We are talking about shipping Canadian wheat to Great Britain, and the possibility of shipping that wheat through a foreign country and obtaining the preference. The Minister of Railways and the Minister of Trade and Commerce both told us how easy it was to do this, but they did not tell us how much grain has been shipped in that way. I want to know if any wheat has been shipped to Great Britain through a foreign country that obtained the preference and, if so, how much.
I have not the figures, but I have made inquiries.

That just goes to show that it is rather hard to do. We were led to believe that most of the grain was going that way, but now we are told that no one knows how much is being shipped through a foreign country.

I said yesterday that I would try to get the figures, and I am still trying to do so. As I pointed out, the movement of grain whether through Buffalo, Montreal or any other export point, is very difficult to keep track of so far as Canadian statistics are concerned. The prevailing practice is to bill the grain out as for the United Kingdom, and then the destination is changed later.
That is not the point.

I am trying to show my
hon. friend the difficulty of securing these figures.

The minister is not
telling us anything we do not know. We are trying to get some actual facts as to how much grain has been shipped in that way, but we are told that no one knows. There is another point I brought up the other day as well. A good deal of our wheat during the past year went to Buffalo and was transshipped to Montreal. We were led to 'believe that practically all Canadian wheat going to Buffalo was shipped in American bottoms. What I should like to know is how much of our wheat
Canada Shipping Act

was shipped in Canadian bottoms and how much in American, going from Buffalo to Montreal. I think you will find that most of it went in Canadian bottoms.

Well, that will not be
interfered with.
It will, I submit, because wheat cannot be shipped in an American bottom to Buffalo and come from Buffalo to Montreal in an American ship.

The hon. gentleman said
that most of the grain went in Canadian bottoms. That will not be interfered with.

We were given to
understand that last year most of the grain went from Buffalo to Montreal in American bottoms, but I contend that most of it went in Canadian ships. This competition is the only competition we have had-the competition furnished by American ships from Buffalo. That is the only competition we have depended on in order to secure low rates. We have been getting low rates because of the fact that grain has come from Buffalo to Montreal in American bottoms. Will the minister tell us how much Canadian wheat going either from Duluth or Chicago to Montreal was carried in Canadian bottoms? We have not had any statement in that regard. Some of the wheat going down the lakes, from Duluth and Chicago, goes down in Canadian bottoms. WThat I want to know is how much wheat during the past year was carried in Canadian ships.

My hon. friend said that
this bill would wipe out the competition so far as Buffalo is concerned. It will not wipe out that competition. It is true it will eliminate part of it but there is still the competition furnished by Canadian ships carrying grain to Buffalo. That competition will continue, and it applies to all grain going on to Montreal or going out the other way. There is still also the competition from the shipping of grain in American bottoms to Buffalo. A man shipping from the head of the lakes may ship in a Canadian bottom to Buffalo, or by an American bottom through an American port, and there is still competition to that extent. The hon. gentleman is correct to this extent, that competition is eliminated with respect to that proportion of the grain that may have been carried to Buffalo in American ships and then carried on to some Canadian port. The fact remains, however, that all competition is not wiped out, because there still remains a good deal of it.

The only competition
we have had for years has been in connection with wheat going to Buffalo. Is not that a fact?
No.

Well, what other competition has there been?
Mr. MANIO'N:	As regards wheat going
to Buffalo-

Let the Minister of
Trade and Commerce answer the question. What competition have our Canadian ships had to face?
Mr. MANIO'N:	The hon. gentleman asks
a question and wishes to answer it himself.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce answered my question. He said no, and I want to know why he gives that answer.

I say that there is still
competition to Buffalo inasmuch as the American ship can take the grain to that port and it can be shipped right through anyway. So that there is still that competition in the shipping of grain from the head of the lakes. The only point is that once it has gone to Buffalo in an American ship it cannot come back to Canada at Montreal, but it can go through Portland, Boston, Philadelphia or New York.

The statement I made was this, that for the last few years the only competition Canadian boats have had to contend with was in connection with grain going to Buffalo, and I said, "Isn't that so?" And the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, "no". Then the Minister of Railways got up to reply to that question I asked. Did he reply to it?
Yes.
I don't think you did. I repeat, the only competition that Canadian boats have had to put up with in the carrying of wheat has been in connection with wheat going to Buffalo. That is all.

And it can still go. to
Buffalo.

I asked whether or not it was so and the Minister of Trade and Commerce said it was not; I was not right. Well, what other competition has there been? Nona whatever. That is the only competition, and that competition to-day is curtailed to a certain

Private Bill
extent because you cannot ship wheat to-day by an American bottom to Buffalo and then on to Montreal; under this bill it cannot be done, so that the competition is curtailed to that extent.

There would have been
no argument if the hon. gentleman had said curtailed in the first instance. I understood him to say that the competition had been wiped out. It is true that it will be curtailed to some extent by this bill, but there is still the Buffalo competition by Canadian boats and on by Canadian boats to Montreal.

The Minister of Trade and
Commerce said that there were a dozen routes by which we could ship from the head of the lakes to Montreal and that only one of them was being interfered with, and that one not completely. That is true, but the one that is being interfered with is the one in which there is competition, and it is the one in which we have lower freight rates. The freight rates to Buffalo are lower than the rates on the shorter haul to bay ports. It is the one in which we have American competition, the one in which we get lower rates; and the result of this interference will be to eliminate the competitive factor which reduces these rates. The minister suggests, further, that there is competition inside the combine-competition among themselves. I say there is not. James Stewart, who is head of the combine, sits in his office and allots the tonnage to the various vessels. He says to one, "You go there and get so many tons", or he may order the ship to tie up and stay where it is. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce will read the bylaws of the company he will appreciate what I am saying. The minister says that there are some lines that are not in the association. Yes; I know one steamship company that refused to be coerced into it because they said it was a direct violation of the criminal code and they would not make themselves liable in that regard. If that is not a combine I do not know what is.

When the hon. gentleman talks about a combine, it reminds me of the time, fifteen years ago, when almost every speech in this house contained references to combines, mergers and so forth. If the hon. gentleman means that certain business groups are working under an arrangement among themselves for the orderly handling of business, and if he suggests that this constitutes a combine, he may interpret the act in that way. But I would point out that there is a definite legal interpretation of the word combine.
Yes, in the criminal code.

In the combines act. A combine exists where there is a combination of business interests in restraint of trade to the detriment of the community as a whole, or affecting other persons' affairs; and under the statute it is competent for any six persons-those who have spoken right in this house-to lay information if they so desire and have an investigation. Such investigations have been held; we have had two or three since the house met. But if my hon. friend talks about a combine in that sense, I say there is none so far as I know. But even in the narrow sense in which he interprets it, I submit that out of forty steamship companies in the business there are twenty-two that are not in the association and eighteen that are, and if we wanted any evidence, if there were any desire to obtain evidence of the ineffectiveness of any combination of interests we have had that evidence in the last two years so far as the welfare of the shipping companies is concerned. We have seen ships tied up, companies going bankrupt, ships not able to get cargoes, and strenuous efforts being put forth to obtain business-keen and bitter competition. There never was a time on the great lakes when there was more competition than there has been in the last year or two. My hon, friend, therefore, should not speak of combines unless he is prepared to make a statement under the act and charge that there is.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.
