The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 106, to amend the Canada Shipping Aot.-Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On subsection 935-British ships only may engage in coasting trade.

Just before six o'clock I was asking the Minister of Trade and Commerce .to tell me how much Canadian wheat had been carried by Canadian bottoms to Montreal and how much Canadian wheat that was in Buffalo had been carried by Canadian bottoms and how much by United States bottoms to Montreal. Has he the information for me now?
I have no additional information.

Just before six o'clock the hon. member for Weybum brought up the matter of the alleged combine. The minister tried to assure us that there was none. Yet he says some eighteen companies were in some sort of association and .there were twenty-two companies that were out of it. That does not give us much information. Would he tell us the amount of tonnage in the association, the amount out of it and also the amount of tonnage interested only in the transportation of wheat. Many boats on tihe lakes will not engage in the transportation of wheat and therefore might not be in this estimate that he gave. As was said by the hon. member for Weyburn, it is well known that James Stewart, who organized this as-

sociation and is the head of it, receives as his share one-fortieth of a cent a bushel for every bushel that is shipped. If he had received his full amount for what Canadian wheat was shipped last year, he would have got in the neighbourhood of $100,000. The wheat growers of western Canada are paying this. To-night's paper shows that the lake freight rate on wheat has fallen to four cents a bushel, this being probaibly due to what took place in the house yesterday. There is some alarm over this legislation. We know very well certain companies thought seriously of going into this association or combine and when they consulted their legal adviser in connection with the matter, he advised them to stay out of it because he said that they would be subject to section 498 of the criminal code which states:
Everyone is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a penalty not exceeding $4,000 and not less than $200, or to two years' imprisonment, or, if a corporation, is liable to a penalty not exceeding $10,000, and not less than $1,000, who conspires, combines, agrees or arranges wph any person, or with any railway, steamship, steamboat or transportation company,
(a) to unduly limit the facilities for transporting, producing, manufacturing, supplying, storing or dealing ip any article or commodity which may be a subject of trade or commerce.
On account of that section, the company to which I have referred was advised not to go into this combine. It is an assured fact that a number of these people are working together for no other purpose than to raise freight rates, that is the only reason they would get together. The only thing which enables us to keep down the prices is the competitive price to Buffalo and under this bill the competition of United States boats going into Buffalo with Canadian grain would be done away with to a great extent. Can the minister give me the information regarding the amount of grain going to Montreal?

As regards the question of tonnage of companies in or out of the association, I have not figured that out at all, but I suppose it could be done without any great difficulty. When I used that argument, I did make the statement that the Canada Steamship Lines, one of the largest companies, was,
I understood, in the association. But I said that there were those twenty-two companies outside, operating independently. I could not give my hon. friend the precise tonnage, but I can say this, that this was in connection with companies engaged in the grain carrying trade.
In regard to the other question asked, namely, the quantity moved from Buffalo to

Canada Shipping Act
Montreal in Canadian vessels and the quantity moved in United States vessels, I made inquiries, but I have not any definite, final figures on the matter, I have not, however, the slightest objection to my hon. friend, for the sake of his argument, assuming what he has or others have asserted, namely, that the bulk of it is carried in Canadian bottoms.
I am not objecting to that at all. I am placing no argument against it. I am not able to give my hon. friend precise figures. When he and other hon. gentlemen ask regarding the amount of grain exported to Great Britain via American ports and that earned the preference, I have told him and others that there is great difficulty in getting those figures. I tried yesterday and the day before to get them, but I have not been able to do so. One of the difficulties, as I pointed out this afternoon, is that frequently, and indeed very . commonly, grain is exported both via Montreal and American ports consigned to the United Kingdom, because that is the best and the largest market, and then frequently after it has left the seaboard it is reconsigned to some other destination. I stated this afternoon that one of the difficulties we have experienced in the compilation of Canadian export statistics is the redirecting of wheat or grain On the high seas after it has left Canadian ports. I am sorry that in- the short time available since this question was raised during the last few days I have not been able to secure the information, although I have asked for it. I am sorry it is not available. It is not a simple but a comparatively difficult matter to work out.

We know that there
have been two shipments of Canadian wheat through foreign ports to Great Britain, and that neither received the preference. We have not heard of any such shipment that did, and therefore we assume, and I believe correctly, that no Canadian wheat so shipped to Great Britain has received the preference in that market. So why beat about the bush? Why not come out openly and say plainly: "We do not know of any such shipment that has received the preference." We have heard of none. We know that two shipments tried to get the preference and did not get it. That is all we have heard about it. On the other hand, it is of vital importance that we should know how much American wheat is taken to Montreal in Canadian bottoms. We hear so much about Canadian wheat going to Buffalo in American bottoms -that I think it is only fair we should be told how much American wheat is taken to Montreal in Cana-53719-330i
dian bottoms. A very large amount of wheat goes out of Montreal every week. How much is Canadian and how much is American?
One more word with regard to this combine. The minister knows very well that this association was started last June, and he also knows very well that at that time the rate from the head of the lakes to Montreal was 4-1 cents. It was the understanding of this association that they would endeavour to put up the rates from Fort William to Montreal half a cent a bushel a month. And how did they succeed? In the month of June the rate from Fort William to Montreal was 4-1; July, 4-5; August, 5-2; September, 6-4; October 6-7 or almost 6-8, and at the very time those rates were being raised by half a cent a bushel a month the rate from Fort William to Buffalo remained steady; it practically never changed at all. Here are the rates from Fort William to Buffalo for the same months: June, 1-56; July, 1-57; August, 1-54; September, 1-52; October, 1-52. So the rates from Fort William to Buffalo practically never changed; and yet the rate from Fort William to Montreal rose from 4-1 in June to almost 6-8 in October. How does the minister explain that, except by the fact that there was some kind of association or combine among the boat owners to raise the rate from the head of the lakes to Montreal? If the minister does not give us any answer we must assume that there was a combine, and I think it is up to the minister and the government to look into that matter.

I did not gather that my hon. friend wanted me to deal with that question again because I have dealt with it already half a dozen times. I have done my utmost to demonstrate to the committee, and I think I have done so to the reasonable satisfaction of hon. members who desire to be fair in the matter, that leaving aside this one rate of four cents which was brought to my attention while I was on my feet, the prevailing rates to-day from Fort William to Montreal are exceedingly reasonable. They are substantially lower than the rates that have prevailed for the last ten years. I gave the rates in detail over a period of ten or twelve years, showing that the prevailing rate of six cents was low. I also pointed out in my previous remarks, but I will repeat it for my hon. friends, that the rate of four cents a bushel is an exceedingly low rate due to distress competition; there is no question about that at all.
I have also pointed out, so far as the alleged combine is concerned, that personally I do not think there is a combine in the sense in
Canada Shipping Act

which that word is used, namely, a combine in restraint of trade. I have also pointed out that the law respecting combines is simple and clear, that any six persons who feel there is a combine in restraint of trade can put the act in motion. The act has been invoked in a number of instances in the last few years, and in a very simple manner. It is not my business to invoke it. It is open to any six citizens who feel in any way aggrieved in that respect to do so.

Suppose six citizens put the act in operation to see if there is a combine. We saw something last year of the effect of that when we had an alleged combine in the coal trade investigated, and we heard nothing more about it.
That is not correct.
Practically speaking. We cannot get the information, anyway.
It is now in the hands of the authorities of Quebec and Ontario.

We would get no better results from an investigation in this case. What I want the minister to explain is how those rates went up. What was the cause of the Canadian boats-and the grain can only be carried in Canadian bottoms-raising the rates from Fort William to Montreal from 4-1 in June to 6-8 in October while the rate from Fort William to Buffalo remained exactly the same during all those months? There is no other reason whatever except the existence of a combine or working arrangement among our Canadian boats to put up the price.

My hon. friend is not stating the case correctly. Wheat can be carried right up to this moment in American bottoms on the first leg of the journey. My hon. friend said that the rise in the rates was due to the fact that the wheat could only be carried in Canadian bottoms. But I say it can be carried in American bottoms. This competition is in existence now and has been in existence. So my hon. friend is not correct in that statement, for there is the full force of American competition at play.
That is just what I wanted the minister to explain-what caused the rise in the rates.

I wish to draw the attention of the minister to a phase that has not so far been discussed. It must be a relief to (Mr. Stevens.]
him to hear something that has not been discussed several times. Subsection 4 of clause 935 reads:
Any goods so transported shall be forfeited as being smuggled goods.
The law is going to forbid a foreign vessel from taking goods or passengers from one port in Canada to another, and it provides a severe penalty for violation of the law, 1500 in the case of freight, and $500 for each passenger in the case of passengers. That may be all right for the big shipping companies and the big shippers who know what the law is, but I submit that to forfeit the goods so transported as being smuggled goods would be very unjust to what is known in some cases as the innocent purchaser. If a man has a horse stolen he can recover it from anybody who has obtained it in an illegal way, but if it is found in the hands of an innocent purchaser who has bought it not knowing it was stolen, and has paid a fair price for it, he cannot recover. Here is a case I should like to place before the minister. Being a business man he may think only in terms of big shipping interests, but I am thinking of the smaller people. I engage his attention, because his local knowledge will enable him to follow me.
We will suppose there is a man at Alert Bay, which is a point one hundred and eighty-three miles north of Vancouver. This man is out of a job, but has a chance to gain employment at Campbell River, a point say, one hundred miles south. He, his wife, his family and household goods are on the wharf at Alert Bay. A steamer comes to that point. He does not ask to see the ship's papers to ascertain where it comes from. Why would he, being a man ignorant of such matters? He goes on board, and when the ship is three or four miles away from the wharf the purser comes along. Of course the purser should not carry the man under those conditions, but chances are he will take him then. A heavy fine may be imposed for this infringement of the law. But I am thinking of the man out of employment. We find that when he gets to Campbell River he is liable to have his household goods forfeited, due to the fact that they are regarded as being smuggled. That is not fair. He has been a perfectly innocent man.
Let me give another instance. A hand logger has been working in a little cove for a period of six months employed getting out logs. He, too, is ignorant of our coastal law. His work is about completed, and he is looking for a tug to tow it to Vancouver, or elsewhere. The cove may be located in a sheltered bay to which tugs would come. Finally he will get

Canada Shipping Act
a fair price from some tug, and that tug is given the work. It is afterwards discovered that he has employed an American tug, and he is liable to forfeit his whole winter's work. It may be argued that this instance would not come under the law, because a tug is not a ship. In answer to that argument I turn to page 10 of the large bill amending the shipping act which, although not yet passed, will no doubt come before us. I find under the definition of a ship that a ship includes "every description of vessel used in navigation, not propelled by oars." Either a tug boat or a gas boat, under that definition, would be a ship. If the man who, in the course of ordinary business, could not be expected to ascertain the exact registry of this tug, does not do so, then he is liable to lose his whole winter's work. That would be the result because of ignorance for which he could not be held responsible. Would it not be sufficient punishment if the ship were fined $500 and a further fine of $500 for each passenger, without confiscating the goods? It seems to me excessive punishment.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
This legislation has been on our statute books for years, and no exception was ever taken to it. There is no change whatever in this clause so far as the points raised by the hon. member are concerned. Clause 935 of the statute reads:
1.	No goods or passengers shall be carried by water, from one port of Canada to another, except in British ships.
2.	If any goods or passengers are so carried, contrary to this part, the master of the ship or vessel so carrying them shall incur a penalty of $400; and any goods so carried shall be forfeited as smuggled.
We have not brought in any new legislation on this point. If the hon. member wishes to read clause 936 he will find that it, also, is fair legislation. The cases suggested by the hon. member are most extreme, and I do not think that such circumstances would ever arise. If they did, I am sure a good lawyer would surely save the goods subject to confiscation, and the owner of the ship would be protected.
I am afraid for the innocent passenger or shipper, not for the owner of the ship. The minister states that this legislation has been in the statutes for years, but never has been enforced.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
It has always been
enforced, but no complaint was ever received against it.

That is equivalent to saying
that in a case such as I have indicated it has never been enforced. If it has never been
enforced this would be a good time to eliminate it. I believe it is good policy to eliminate faulty legislation when we are making a general revision. If it cannot be defended more successfully than the minister has defended it, I suggest my contention holds. The minister has stated that I have referred to extreme cases. I say that they are not extreme, but are common cases in the area in which I am interested, and are likely to occur at any time. I cannot definitely point out any cases in which the law has been enforced, but it is not wise to have useless legislation on the statute books. However, if the minister will not listen to me I shall not waste the time of the committee.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Merchant Shipping Act 1894, not affected.

I have only one last word
to say to the minister. On this bill which contains only two sections there has been a discussion lasting about three hours and a half. This lengthy discussion has been brought about because the bill was not sent to a committee where it could have been discussed around a table. I have in my hand the original bill which no doubt will be introduced again next year. This bill containing amendments to the shipping act consists of eight hundred and twenty-one sections, and by a simple process of arithmetic I have ascertained that if we are as long proportionately in the discussion of that bill as we have been on this one, about ten months' continuous sitting will be required. I submit to the minister, and to the Prime Minister, who, I suppose, is in some measure responsible for the present bill being brought 'before a committee of the whole instead of before the special committee, that they would do well to allow the bigger bill to go to the committee on marine and fisheries. I believe it is within the knowledge of every hon. member who has followed the progress of bills, such as the pension bill, that legislation is passed much more quickly if in the first instance it is discussed before the smaller committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I can say to my
hon. friend that the matter will be considered then. I do not think so much time will be required for the study of the full revision, because a great many of the sections are merely a repetition of sections in force at the present time. Some parts of the bill may be contested, but many of them will be accepted as being the law in force at the present time.

Section agreed to.
Business of the House

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have an amendment which I shall ask my colleague to move.

The government has decided and the minister is now asking me to move an amendment which the Prime Minister suggests should be added as a third section at the end of the bill, as follows:
That subsection 12 of section 1 of this act shall come into force on a date to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council published in the Canada Gazette.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What it is intended to do is to add a section providing that subsection 12 of section 1, which reenacts section 935 regarding British ships only engaging in coasting trade, shall come into force only on proclamation. It will be a new section 3.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time on division and passed.

subtopic: PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING-REDISTRIBUTION BILL-ADJOURNMENT UNTIL MONDAY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING-REDISTRIBUTION BILL-ADJOURNMENT UNTIL MONDAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, shortly after three o'clock this afternoon I indicated that the notice *standing in my name on the order paper [DOT]might stand until eight o'clock. That notice is of a motion that the house sit to-morrow from eleven to one o'clock and from three mntil six, and probably not in the evening. I Shave just been conferring with the right hon. leader of the opposition, who takes the view that it is perhaps undesirable that we should sit to-morrow. I am prepared to sit to-morrow and start consideration of the redistribution bill. The first seven sections of it I fancy could be passed without difficulty, and I then propose to commence at page 34 of the schedule and take the ridings in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, in Manitoba, British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta, leaving Ontario and Quebec only for further consideration. I am entirely in the hands of the house in the matter, and will be guided largely by the views that are expressed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE ICING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING-REDISTRIBUTION BILL-ADJOURNMENT UNTIL MONDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if
we had been fortunate enough to reach an agreement that was at all general with respect to the redistribution measure I would see some advantage in going on immediately with the bill. But if, as I understand is the case, no agreement has been reached between the different parties in the house with respect to

the constituencies generally, I think possibly it would be just as well to conclude everything except the redistribution measure and start afresh with it on Monday morning.
The Prime Minister speaks as though it is going to be an easy matter to pass the bill, but I may say to him at once that if what has been accomplished in the last three redistributions, namely effecting a redistribution by agreement, is not to be accomplished at the present time, I am afraid we will have to take as strong a position as we can in this matter, and while we may be in the minority we will do the best we can to protect the rights of the minority and if need be fight to the finish. If the choice is to lie between a redistribution to be effected by joint agreement of the different parties in the house and one which is to be put through, as the Prims Minister said the other day, by "what is sometimes called the brute majority," we will just have to see how long we can resist the brute majority. We certainly are not going to see the constituencies of this country unjustly redistributed at the will of the administration just because they know they have the majority behind them to put any redistribution through. I had hoped that it might be possible to effect a redistribution in the different provinces of the dominion that would be recognized as fair, but apparently that is not the case, and in the circumstances I would say-having in mind that we have done our best this week to make progress, we have for some time past been sitting morning, afternoon and night- that we might very well adjourn until Monday next and begin on the redistribution measure then. If hon. gentlemen opposite want to begin at once with their brute majority, let them go ahead.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING-REDISTRIBUTION BILL-ADJOURNMENT UNTIL MONDAY
speechtext: All of which, Mr. Speaker, sounds well, but we are dealing with actualities. A very earnest effort has been made for weeks to find an accommodation with respect to these ridings. If there has been disagreement with respect to at least one of the provinces it is because we know that they never intended to agree; they have been good enough to so express themselves privately, at least, if not publicly-privately in the sense that it was not said on the floor of this house, but nevertheless publicly so far as the purport of it was concerned. I have no desire that there should be placed upon the statute book an unfair redistribution, but I will not become a party to an unfair redistribution being put on the statute book by the will of the minority.

subtopic: PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING-REDISTRIBUTION BILL-ADJOURNMENT UNTIL MONDAY
speechtext:
We never asked that.

Business oj the House

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING-REDISTRIBUTION BILL-ADJOURNMENT UNTIL MONDAY
speechtext:
That is exactly what is
asked, and nothing else. It has been said, for instance, that the difficulty is with regard to agreement. There is no disagreement about New Brunswick; it loses one member. No county boundaries have been disturbed; nothing has been done except to drop one member from Saint John. In the province of Nova Scotia, because of the desire to maintain county boundaries as they exist at present, one of our own members finds himself living in a constituency that has fifty thousand people. He has made sacrifices in that direction which he says will legislate him out of the House of Commons. That does not look like jerrymandering. In the province of Prince Edward Island there has been no change at all. At least fifty of the seats in Ontario have been agreed upon beyond all question, and at least seventy-five seats have been agreed upon in a reasonable way.
It has been pointed out that many changes have been made in Quebec. Why? Because for the first time in the history of this dominion we have the urban population constituting a majority of the people. The burden cast upon those responsible for redistribution has been correspondingly great. Need I point out that the island of Montreal contains practically ten per cent of the population of this country; if it received ten per cent of the seats it would have twenty-four members. That brings about a great difficulty, and the city of Toronto stands in somewhat the same position. With respect to Manitoba an agreement has been arrived at; no one is complaining, so why should not the schedule be adopted? In Saskatchewan there were two proposals submitted, one by those who had given much thought and attention to .the figures and the other by hon. gentlemen opposite. Finally the matter resolved itself into smaller differences. A great agitation was carried on because the seat of the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) was being taken away. As a matter of fact the majority of the members of the committee said, "We will yield that point and be done with it, rather than waste time." But as soon ias that was done something else cropped up. We will never be able to do business in that way; that is certain. There were some differences in Alberta, one of them because an hon. member has moved his place of residence:, and he wants the place where he now lives to be included in the constituency which he represents. He might move again to-morrow. Should the constituency be changed again in that event?

subtopic: PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING-REDISTRIBUTION BILL-ADJOURNMENT UNTIL MONDAY
speechtext:
That is
absurd.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING-REDISTRIBUTION BILL-ADJOURNMENT UNTIL MONDAY
speechtext:
It was absurd, I quite
agree; it was absurd for many reasons, some of which I shall be glad to discuss in this house when the time comes. Then there was the province of British Columbia, where there were two or three minor differences, one being the question of whether a portion of the territory on the mainland should be included in the constituency of Comox-Albemi or in another constituency. There were also some differences in regard to the city of Vancouver, and that territory was divided according to the boundaries established for provincial constituencies. Since the lists are made under circumstances with which the house is familiar it does seem to me that this was not an unreasonable way of dealing with the situation.
Personally I am bound to say that I have not followed the details of this redistribution question, though this afternoon I made myself perhaps more familiar with them than I have been heretofore. I was of the opinion that if we adopted the schedules with respect to the other provinces we might be ablq, in connect-tion with Ontario and Quebec, to arrive at an accommodation that would more nearly represent what everyone, including our opponents opposite, would feel was reasonable. But it is difficult; no one who has not been through this matter understands just how difficult it is. Twenty years ago I was a member of the committee that dealt with redistribution when Sir Robert Borden was in power. I recall the difficulties and the differences that manifested themselves at that time, with members finding themselves out of their constituencies, and I am bound to say that it was not until the last two or three days that we finally managed to have matters disposed of. At that time, however, the rural population was more numerous than the urban population and the difficulties were not so great as they are now. Perhaps the very conditions under which we live, world conditions of depression, tend to create a certain state of mind on the part of members of the House of Commons who sit opposite a government as well as on the part of those who sit on the government side; that may be responsible for part of it. If it is thought that it will conduce to a fair and reasonable discussion of these matters I shall not press that the house sit to-morrow. Personally I think it should, but in this instance as in many others I am willing to yield to what the opposition may think desirable in the national interest.
I do not wish to speak at length with regard to this matter; I have only one further word
Business oj the House

to say. In the very nature of things, when you have had one party completely dominating the position in a province or provinces for many years you are bound to have difficulties when you come to the question of redistribution, when the voice of what is still the minority in those provinces but which constitutes a part of the majority in parliament is heard. The very fact that it is a minority voice in those particular provinces but is a part of the majority voice in parliament makes the position doubly difficult, and in my judgment a frank recognition of that fact is desirable. If a peaceful solution of our problems can be found, well and good, but I think that peaceful solution will be found more readily by proceeding with the bill and meeting the difficulties when we come to them, endeavouring to dispose of them as men should at such a time.
I desire to add only this, that it is always She privilege of a minority, or the opposition in parliament, to keep the house in session just as long as it reasonably can. During the short time I have been here I have made it a rule to be neither deterred by threats nor influenced by promises in the conduct of the business of this house, and I say to hon. gentlemen that I shall not be deterred from doing what I conceive to be my duty with respect to redistribution either by the threat of being kept here or the promise that if I do not do my duty we will not be kept here. We shall continue along the course we have mapped out, and carry forward a fair and equitable redistribution of the seats in parliament.

subtopic: PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING-REDISTRIBUTION BILL-ADJOURNMENT UNTIL MONDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, being a man of peace, as my right hon. friend from Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) knows, I do not wish to add fuel to the flame by discussing the fairness or unfairness of the proposals contained in the bill as it has come back from the committee. I do not think it is desirable that we should do so this evening.
May I say that I think it is always very desirable, if it is at all possible, to have an agreement between the parties in this house as to the redistribution scheme which will be finally carried out, but I desire to say to my right hon. friend that it will be impossible to proceed with this bill as he suggests. The right hon. gentleman suggested that we might adopt the first seven sections of the bill and then consider some of the schedules as to which there does not seem to be much
tMr. Bennett.]
disagreement. We cannot accept section 3; that is the whole point of contention. Section 3 reads:
The said provinces and territory respectively shall, for the purposes of the election of members to serve in the House of Commons, be divided into electoral districts, and be represented as provided in the schedule to this act.
Those who object to part of the schedules cannot vote for this section; certainly the whole discussion will be made on section 3 of the bill. As to the other sections, I agree that they are not contentious, but wre cannot discuss section 3 unless every possibility of agreement has disappeared. So far as I am concerned, I shall not be able to leave my place in the house while this bill is being considered. I have been summoned to attend this evening a meeting of what have been called the elderly statesmen. I am proud of the last word, though not of the first, because it is not right as applied to myself. But I could not attend that meeting if this bill were being considered by the committee. I urge upon the Prime Minister the advisability of accepting the suggestion of the right hon. the leader of the opposition, so that we might try to find out definitely whether we can agree, as every one hopes we shall, and then if we cannot we can discuss the bill on Monday. May I point out that some of us are rather tired at the close of this week. Speaking for myself, and I know that the same is true of others, we have all done pretty strenuous work this week and I do not think it is fair to ask that we should begin the consideration of the bill to-night.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING-REDISTRIBUTION BILL-ADJOURNMENT UNTIL MONDAY
speechtext: In that event I would move that the house do now adjourn.

subtopic: PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING-REDISTRIBUTION BILL-ADJOURNMENT UNTIL MONDAY
speechtext:
I understand that the Prime Minister was just about to move the adjournment of the house. Unfortunately, when this question was brought up, I was waiting upstairs for the special committee of this house to meet, but I believe that the leader of the opposition suggested that the house should not meet to-morrow, his reason being that we might have the weekend to explore the situation further in the hope of arriving at some reasonable conclusion. I must confess that my experience of this committee has been a unique one. I have seen party strife at play to the greatest extent one could imagine, but, notwithstanding that, I consider that the committee had made splendid progress. Unfortunately to-day

Questions
the committee was able to meet only for a short time; because of other duties intervening we were unable to meet this afternoon. I am quite confident however that if the major parties of the house agree to restrain themselves and be calm on the subject we can arrive at a fairly satisfactory solution of the problem which will be beneficial to all concerned. I merely rose to say to the Prime Minister that I think he would be well advised to move the adjournment of the house over the week-end for the purpose of having further parleys with a view to arriving at a reasonable conclusion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING-REDISTRIBUTION BILL-ADJOURNMENT UNTIL MONDAY
speechtext: I move that the house do now adjourn until Monday at eleven a.m.; the motion is seconded by Sir George Perley. Possibly there is very much in what has been said, namely, that the expression to-night of strong views and the rousing perhaps of latent passions in connection with a matter of this kind could serve no useful purpose, and we might be further ahead on Monday morning than if we proceeded to-night.

subtopic: PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING-REDISTRIBUTION BILL-ADJOURNMENT UNTIL MONDAY
speechtext:
I think so.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 8.55 p.m.
Monday, May 22, 1933
